claims.text: Sufficient chromium promotes formation of a protective passive film on steel.
The protective film is a Cr-based oxide.
The Cr-based film reforms continuously after local damage.
Film reformation maintains corrosion resistance in high-temperature, high-pressure chemical-processing or nuclear environments.
The proposed study varies steel chromium content over approximately 10–18 wt% while controlling minor alloying elements such as Mo and Ni.
In-situ X-ray and localized electrochemical measurements during exposure and deliberate film damage can test oxide formation and recovery.
The targeted service-like conditions are aqueous environments at 250–350 °C and pressures up to about 10 MPa, potentially containing LiOH and boric acid.
The passivating structure is a dual-layer, chromium-enriched oxide or spinel containing FeCr2O4.
The passivating layer may contain Mo-rich and Ni-rich constituents.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes at flawed or damaged surface regions.
Preferential chromium oxidation rebuilds a dense protective oxide over breakdown sites and prevents sustained corrosive attack.
Steels with sufficient chromium will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than steels with insufficient chromium.
Increasing chromium content raises the pitting potential.
Chromium-rich steels will exhibit rapid repassivation after deliberate oxide-film disruption.
Low-chromium or carbon-steel controls will show rising corrosion currents and little or no rapid passivation recovery under identical conditions.
The proposed protective behavior requires approximately 10–12 wt% chromium or more, with the threshold depending on co-alloying.
The mechanism should hold under moderate pH and temperature conditions typical of chemical-processing or nuclear-power operations.
Extremely low or high pH and temperatures beyond design envelopes may degrade oxide self-healing.
The effects of Mo, Ni, W, and radiation on oxide self-repair rates are not fully understood.
Failure of steels containing at least 10–12 wt% Cr to repair the film or outperform low-Cr controls under matched conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
